acceptedAnswer.text: Erectile dysfunction (ED) is recurring difficulty getting or keeping an erection firm enough for sex. Occasional changes happen; when they become a pattern, it may be worth evaluating why.
There isn’t one cause. Blood flow, cardiovascular and metabolic health, hormones, medications, nerve function, stress, and other factors can all contribute — sometimes together.

mainEntity.name: Is erectile dysfunction always caused by low testosterone?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Testosterone can play a role, but ED can also be related to circulation, metabolic health, medications, stress, nerve function, and other factors. That’s why one hormone test rarely tells the whole story.

mainEntity.name: What’s the difference between low libido and erectile dysfunction?

acceptedAnswer.text: Low libido means reduced sexual desire. Erectile dysfunction affects the ability to get or maintain an erection. They can happen together, but one doesn’t necessarily mean you have the other.

mainEntity.name: Is erectile dysfunction permanent, or can it improve?

acceptedAnswer.text: That depends on what’s contributing to it. ED has many possible causes, and treatment may involve addressing an underlying health issue as well as improving sexual function. Your physician can help determine what applies in your case.

mainEntity.name: What does an erectile dysfunction evaluation actually check?

acceptedAnswer.text: It starts with more than testosterone. At RHM, we look at your symptoms and history alongside hormonal, metabolic, cardiovascular, thyroid, and general health markers to understand the broader picture.
